Guideline: Know which caching model the app uses
Description: Next.js 16 has two caching models. With cacheComponents enabled, data fetching is dynamic by default, you opt in with the 'use cache' directive plus cacheLife and cacheTag, and Partial Prerendering is the default behavior (experimental.ppr and experimental_ppr were removed). Without it, the previous model applies: fetch is uncached unless opted in, and route segment config such as dynamic, revalidate and fetchCache still works. Check next.config before choosing an API.
Do: Read next.config first; use 'use cache' with cacheComponents, fetch options and segment config without it
Don't: Mix the two models or enable experimental.ppr in Next.js 16
Code Good: // cacheComponents: true async function getPosts() { 'use cache'; cacheLife('max'); return db.posts.findMany(); }
Code Bad: experimental: { ppr: true } // removed in Next.js 16; PPR comes from cacheComponents

Description: Fetch directly in async Server Components
Do: async function Page() { const data = await fetch() }

Guideline: Opt fetch into caching explicitly (previous model)
Description: Without Cache Components, fetch requests are not cached by default. Opt in per request with cache: 'force-cache' or next: { revalidate: seconds }, and tag requests with next: { tags } for on-demand revalidation.
Do: cache: 'force-cache' or next: { revalidate } where data may be cached
Don't: Assume an unconfigured fetch is cached
Code Good: fetch(url, { cache: 'force-cache' }) // or { next: { revalidate: 3600, tags: ['posts'] } }

Description: Server Actions for form submissions

After a mutation, revalidatePath(path) or revalidateTag(tag, profile). Since Next.js 16 revalidateTag requires a cacheLife profile as its second argument (the one-argument form is deprecated). In Server Actions, updateTag expires and refreshes the tag in the same request so the user sees their own write.
Do: revalidateTag(tag, 'max') or updateTag(tag) in a Server Action after mutating
Don't: revalidateTag(tag) without a profile, or router.refresh() after every mutation
Code Good: revalidatePath('/posts'); revalidateTag('posts', 'max'); // read-your-writes in a Server Action: updateTag('posts')
Code Bad: revalidateTag('posts') // single-argument form deprecated in Next.js 16

Guideline: Await params, searchParams, cookies() and headers()
Description: Since Next.js 16, synchronous access to request APIs is removed: params (in layouts, pages, route handlers and metadata image files), searchParams (in pages), cookies(), headers() and draftMode() must be awaited. PageProps and LayoutProps helpers generated by next typegen type them.
Do: await params and searchParams; await cookies() and headers()
Don't: Read params.slug or call cookies().get() synchronously
Code Good: export default async function Page({ params }: PageProps<'/blog/[slug]'>) { const { slug } = await params; }
Code Bad: export default function Page({ params }) { const slug = params.slug; } // removed in Next.js 16

Guideline: Preload only the LCP image; priority is deprecated
Description: Starting with Next.js 16 the priority prop is deprecated in favor of preload, which inserts a preload link in <head>. Use it only for the single Largest Contentful Paint image and not together with loading or fetchPriority. The docs say loading="eager" or fetchPriority="high" is preferable in most cases.
Do: fetchPriority="high" or preload on the one LCP image
Don't: priority (deprecated) or preload on several images

Guideline: Use proxy.ts for optimistic checks only
Description: Next.js 16 renamed middleware.ts to proxy.ts (export function proxy). Proxy runs on the Node.js runtime and the runtime cannot be configured; middleware.ts is deprecated and only kept for the edge runtime. The authentication guide treats Proxy as optional: read the session cookie for optimistic redirects, avoid database checks because it runs on every matched route including prefetches, and never make it the only line of defense. CVE-2025-29927 showed middleware checks could be bypassed in unpatched versions.
Do: proxy.ts for cookie-based redirects; verify auth again close to the data
Don't: Treat proxy or middleware as the authorization boundary, or query the database in it
Code Good: // proxy.ts export function proxy(request: NextRequest) { if (!request.cookies.has('session')) return NextResponse.redirect(new URL('/login', request.url)); }
Code Bad: // middleware.ts is the only auth check; pages, Server Actions and Route Handlers trust the request

Description: Without a matcher, proxy runs on every request, including _next/static, _next/image and public assets, so redirects can block CSS, JS or images. Exclude them with a negative-lookahead matcher. Server Functions are POST requests to the route where they are used, so a matcher that skips a path also skips its Server Function calls.
Don't: Run proxy on every request without a matcher
Code Bad: // no matcher: proxy also runs for static files and optimized images

Guideline: Authorize in a Data Access Layer
Description: Put session verification in a server-only Data Access Layer (for example verifySession wrapped in React cache) and call it from data requests, Server Actions and Route Handlers. Layouts do not re-render on navigation and do not stop nested segments from rendering, so returning null from a layout is not protection.
Do: Call a server-only verifySession() wherever data is read or mutated
Don't: Rely on a layout check or on proxy alone
Code Good: export const verifySession = cache(async () => { const session = await decrypt((await cookies()).get('session')?.value); if (!session?.userId) redirect('/login'); return session; });
Code Bad: // layout.tsx: if (!session) return null — nested pages and Server Actions still run
